{{< include _arrange-kit.qmd >}}

A story song can be well written and still fall flat if it is sung like a list. The singer is the narrator, and every choice of volume, speed and colour tells the listener
what the narrator feels. This lesson is about those choices. For voice technique itself (breath, mix, safe belting) see [Pop Singing](voice-pop.qmd), and for floating words over the beat, [Jazz Singing: back-phrasing a ballad](voice-jazz.qmd#back-phrasing-a-ballad).

::: {.vx-care}
**Look after your voice.** Warm up first. Stop if anything hurts or feels tight. Quiet, close singing is not safer than loud singing if you squeeze to make it.
:::

## 1. Speak it first

Before you sing a word, **say the verse** as if telling it to a friend. Notice where you naturally pause, which words you lean on, where you speed up, and where you slow down. That is the shape of the story.
The melody should serve that shape, not replace it.

**Task.** Say your verse aloud twice: once flat, once as if it really happened to you. Mark the words that changed.

## 2. Choose the words that land

In every line there is one word that carries the meaning. Singers put the weight there: a little longer, a little louder, or a little quieter and closer. Mark it on your lyric sheet.

Rule of thumb: **one word per line**, two at the most. If everything is stressed, nothing is.

## 3. Breathe where the sense breaks

Take a breath at a comma or a change of thought, not in the middle of a phrase. A breath before an important word is also a way of **warning the listener** that something is coming. And a breath that is *not* taken, a phrase run straight on, can sound like a story getting out of control.

## 4. Verse is close, chorus is open

A common plan, and the one the band uses ([Story Songs 2](story-music.qmd)):

| | Verse | Chorus |
|---|---|---|
| **Volume** | quieter | fuller |
| **Distance from the mic** | closer, more breath | a little back |
| **Tone** | speech-like, plain | rounder, longer vowels |
| **Rhythm** | follows the words, may be loose | firmer, closer to the beat |
| **Feeling** | telling someone | telling everyone |

And the last chorus is often the most different: bigger, or the opposite, so quiet that it has to be listened to.

## 5. Ends of words

In a ballad the **last consonants** (d, t, s) carry meaning. A tidy end to a word makes a line sound sure; a dropped end makes it sound tired or tender. Decide which you want for each line, and be consistent.
At the mic, see [Recording 2: pops and esses](rec-voice.qmd#pops-and-esses).

## 6. Sing over a ballad

Sing (or speak in rhythm) over this backing. Take the chords from the loop you used in [Story Songs 5](story-lyric.qmd). Switch the instruments off in turn to hear how much room the voice has with fewer players.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="pop" data-chart="C|G|Am|F|C|G|Am|F" data-tempo="68" data-comp="piano" data-on="comp bass" data-staves="comp"></div>

At 68 beats per minute each bar is a little under 3.5 seconds. Count how many words you can say comfortably in a bar. That is your line length.

## 7. Record two takes and compare

1. Record the verse and chorus on your phone, **once with every word equal**, then **once with your marked words landed, breaths planned, verse close and chorus open**.
2. Listen on headphones. For each take, write one sentence: *what does the narrator feel?*
3. Which take tells the story better? Which single change made the difference?
4. Keep both, named and dated, in your [process journal](process-journal.qmd). Two versions and a reason is evidence of exploring ideas for Criterion B.

## 8. If you are not the singer

You may write the song and give it to another voice. Then say in writing **what you want**: which words, how close, how loud. Or sit with them at the mic. A narrator has to believe the story, so tell them what you meant.

Back to the beginning: [Story Songs 1: Songs That Tell Stories](story-songs.qmd).
